newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech communists dismiss NATO nuclear gesture.
newsitem.headline: Czech communists dismiss NATO nuclear gesture.

text.p: The last communist defence minister of a united Czechoslovakia on Thursday dismissed NATO assurances that it would not station nuclear weapons in former East Bloc countries, saying his party remained opposed to expanding the Western alliance.

General Miroslav Vacek, once a top Warsaw Pact general, said that if a crisis developed NATO could rapidly move nuclear arms into the Czech Republic, which became a separate state when Czechoslovakia split in 1993.
On Tuesday NATO confirmed it would recruit new members from the former communist bloc by 1999, and tried to pacify Moscow by saying it had no plans to station nuclear arms in the East.
But Vacek, who was defence minister in a transitional administration after the 1989 fall of communism, said this would do nothing to weaken communist opposition to expansion.
"This proclamation cannot change our opinions about NATO," Vacek, now a senior communist member of parliament, told a news conference.

"If NATO creates infrastructure necessary for the transfer of these weapons in crisis situations, then their deployment on the territory of new members can be done in just several hours," said Vacek, who was Czechoslovakia's chief of the general staff before the 1989 "Velvet Revolution".

Vacek is a member of the Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia, successor to the party which ruled the former Czechoslovakia for 41 years, which won 11 percent of the vote in parliamentary elections eralier this year.
While the government is determined to gain early NATO membership, opinion polls show ordinary Czechs are much more sceptical than many of their fellow central Europeans.

One recent poll showed 38 percent supported the idea but 35 percent opposed it, with the rest undecided. Czechs, who hosted Soviet unclear weapons until after the Velvet Revolution, are particularly strongly against NATO doing likewise.

Vacek, who was defence minister in 1989-90, raised the possibility of nuclear counter-strikes. "Those who allow such a deployment must be aware that right after their deployment, whenever it is done, these installations will become first-wave targets to be destroyed," he said.
President Vaclav Havel created a stir last year by suggesting that joining NATO could mean, at least theoretically, alliance nuclear wepaons being stationed on Czech territory.
